reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Late-onset muscular dystrophy, usually autosomal dominant, caused by a short GCN trinucleotide repeat expansion in PABPN1 encoding poly(A)-binding protein nuclear 1
Typically presents in mid-to-late adulthood with progressive ptosis and dysphagia as the cardinal features
Ptosis is usually bilateral and slowly progressive, and patients often adopt a head-tilt-back posture to see beneath the drooping lids
Dysphagia progresses over time and predisposes to aspiration, weight loss, and malnutrition, which are the main sources of morbidity
Proximal limb-girdle weakness, particularly of the pelvic girdle, develops later in the disease course
External ophthalmoplegia may occur but is usually mild and rarely causes troublesome diplopia
Diagnosis is confirmed by targeted repeat-expansion testing of PABPN1, supported by the characteristic clinical picture

Management is supportive, with swallowing assessment and dietary modification, aspiration precautions, and surgical options such as ptosis correction and cricopharyngeal intervention for selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy is caused by a modest expansion of a GCN repeat in PABPN1, which lengthens the polyalanine tract of the poly(A)-binding protein nuclear 1. The mutant protein misfolds and aggregates into intranuclear inclusions within muscle-fibre nuclei, disturbing RNA processing and polyadenylation. The selective vulnerability of the levator palpebrae, pharyngeal, and later proximal limb muscles produces the characteristic combination of progressive ptosis, dysphagia, and eventual limb-girdle weakness. Aggregate accumulation over decades accounts for the late onset and slow progression.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial disease with chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia
Thyroid eye disease causing ptosis or ophthalmoplegia
Motor neurone disease with bulbar involvement
additionalInvestigations: Targeted repeat-expansion genetic testing of PABPN1
Serum creatine kinase, which is normal or mildly elevated
Muscle biopsy with characteristic intranuclear inclusions in selected cases
Nutritional assessment and monitoring of weight
redFlags: Recurrent aspiration or aspiration pneumonia from progressive dysphagia
Ptosis obscuring vision and impairing safe mobility
Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting an alternative diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Progression is slow and life expectancy is often near normal, but dysphagia-related complications such as aspiration and malnutrition are the principal threats to health. Proactive swallowing management and timely surgical intervention improve quality of life and reduce aspiration risk.
pitfalls: Mistaking the ptosis and ophthalmoplegia for myasthenia gravis and giving inappropriate treatment
Underestimating the aspiration risk from progressive dysphagia
Overlooking the family history given the autosomal dominant late-onset pattern
Neglecting nutritional assessment as swallowing deteriorates
Failing to consider the diagnosis in older adults presenting with isolated ptosis
management: No disease-modifying drug exists; management is supportive and directed principally at the ptosis and dysphagia
Ptosis corrected surgically with blepharoplasty or frontalis-sling suspension to restore the visual field and relieve the compensatory head-tilt-back posture
Dysphagia managed with swallowing rehabilitation, texture-modified diet and cricopharyngeal myotomy or dilatation in selected patients
Nutritional support with dietetic input, escalating to gastrostomy feeding when aspiration or malnutrition becomes severe
Aspiration prevention through instrumental swallowing assessment, upright feeding, chest physiotherapy and prompt treatment of respiratory infection
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and mobility aids for the later proximal limb-girdle weakness, with periodic weight and swallowing surveillance
Multidisciplinary neuromuscular care coordinating neurology, ENT/OMFS, speech and language therapy, dietetics and ophthalmology
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant PABPN1 disorder, with predictive testing and family screening
